title: Introduction
text:
Every summer and winter, football clubs hand over tons and tons of money for players, and the number attached to each transfer rarely feels arbitrary - yet it’s remarkably hard to pin down where that number actually comes from. A 22 year-old defender might be valued at 15 million euros while a similarly aged midfielder down the road goes for a fraction of that, and the difference often comes down to a mix of factors that even seasoned football people struggle to fully untangle. For most of the sport’s history, this kind of judgment lived entirely in the heads of scouts - people who spent weekends in the stands, watched tape late into the night, and trusted their gut more than any spreadsheet. That’s shifted quite a bit over the past decade or so, as clubs have started tracking an enormous amount about their players: how many goals they score, how many minutes they log, how often they get called up to their national team, even how disciplined they are on the pitch. Services that specialize in estimating a player’s transfer value have become part of how the football world talks about talent, showing up in newspaper headlines and fan debates just as often as in boardrooms. Well-known valuation platforms, most notably Transfermarkt’s own market value estimates and the CIES Football Observatory’s player valuation models, have become widely cited reference points across the sport, even though the exact reasoning behind any single number is rarely made fully transparent.
The stakes are real for everyone involved - a club that misjudges a signing can set itself back for years, a player’s earning power hinges on how the market perceives them, and agents build entire careers around negotiating that gap between perceived and actual worth. Still, valuing a player is nowhere close to a solved problem. Age plays a role, but so does position, physical build, the league a player competes in, and even reputation built up over time - and it’s genuinely unclear how much weight each of these should carry, or how they interact with one another. A 20 year-old striker and a 32 year-old goalkeeper aren’t judged by the same yardstick, and a player who looks average by the numbers might still be considered invaluable for reasons that never show up in a stat sheet. It’s this tangle of overlapping, sometimes contradictory signals that makes player valuation such a genuinely interesting problem to dig into.
Football is harder to measure than most sports. In baseball, almost everything that happens can be counted. In football, a midfielder’s best moment might be a pass that never shows up as an assist, and a defender’s best game might be one where nothing seemed to happen. Clubs now have analytics teams working next to their scouts, and people whose whole job is turning match footage into numbers. The hope is that stats and human judgment together beat either one alone, and that smaller clubs can find players that bigger clubs miss. Whether that is really working, and what a fair price for a player is, still gets argued over every transfer window. For clubs, players and fans, knowing what drives a player’s value matters because it decides who gets signed, who gets sold and what a club can afford next.

title: Clustering
text:
Clustering is a way to group things that look alike without telling the computer what the groups are. Every player is a row of numbers, and the method puts players with similar numbers together. Since nobody supplies the answer, it works well for finding patterns that were not obvious before.
There are two main styles. In partitional clustering, like k-means, the number of groups (k) is chosen first. The method places k centers in the data, assigns each player to the closest center, moves each center to the middle of its group, and repeats until nothing changes. In hierarchical clustering, every player starts as their own group, and the two closest groups are merged over and over until only one is left. The merges are drawn as a tree called a dendrogram, and cutting the tree at any height gives a set of clusters.
Both styles need a way to measure how close two players are. K-means here uses regular straight-line (Euclidean) distance. The hierarchical clustering uses cosine distance, which looks at the pattern of a player’s numbers instead of how big they are, and it joins groups using the average distance between their members (average linkage).
The plan is to use clustering to look for types of players without ever giving position as an input. If the groups match attackers, defenders and goalkeepers, position shows up on its own in the numbers. If they don’t, something else, like age or international experience, is doing the sorting. Position is only checked afterward.
K-means with three centroids (black X) on 300 players, using goals per 90 minutes and market value. Each player goes to the closest center, and the centers move until nothing changes.
A dendrogram for 25 randomly chosen players, built by merging the closest groups step by step. The taller a join is, the further apart the merged groups were.

title: Data Prep & EDA
text:
Data for this project comes from two sources. The primary dataset is a large, regularly updated collection of European soccer data covering player profiles, appearances, and market valuations, downloaded from Kaggle. It provided detailed player-level information - including position, physical attributes, career statistics, and valuation history - spanning tens of thousands of professional players. This was supplemented with data pulled directly from the football-data.org API, which provides live standings and match information for major competitions, adding current-season context alongside the historical player data. Player age was also added as a new column, worked out from each player’s date of birth to the date of their most recent valuation, so it lines up with the market value.
The combined dataset required meaningful cleaning before analysis. Player performance statistics were aggregated from individual match appearances into career totals, and the most recent market valuation for each player was identified from a full valuation history. Missing values were handled differently depending on what they represented: players with no recorded match appearances were removed, since no performance analysis was possible for them, while smaller gaps in fields like preferred foot or birth country were filled with an explicit “Unknown” label rather than guessed. A data entry error was also identified and corrected, where two players had implausible height values that appeared to be a unit mismatch in the source data. A small number of players (62, under 1% of the dataset) had their position listed as “Missing” in the original source data - this was retained as-is given its negligible size rather than dropped or guessed. After cleaning, the dataset consisted of just over 27,000 players with complete, usable records across all key fields.

Exploratory Visualizations



Distribution of player market values


Player market values are heavily right-skewed, with most players valued under 1 million euros and a long tail of elite players reaching 100 million euros or more.



Market value by position


Median valuations are broadly similar across positions, though attackers and midfielders show a wider spread and higher ceiling among top earners.



Player age vs. market value


Median value rises from about 300,000 euros at ages 18 to 20 to around 500,000 euros in the mid-twenties, stays there until about 28, then falls to about 100,000 euros by 37 to 38. Age is measured at each player’s most recent valuation.



Career goals vs. assists by position


Attackers cluster toward high goal counts while midfielders and defenders show relatively higher assist contributions for their goal totals.



Top 10 clubs by average player market value


Paris Saint-Germain, Real Madrid, and Manchester City lead all clubs in average player valuation, reflecting their concentration of high-value talent.



Average market value by preferred foot


Left-footed players show a modestly higher average market value than right-footed players, though both fall within overlapping confidence ranges.



Correlation between key player metrics


Market value is only weakly related to the other metrics (0.23 to 0.29), and slightly negative with age (-0.16). Games, goals, assists and minutes are strongly linked to each other, since players who play more pile up more of everything.



Top 15 nationalities by player count


Spain, Brazil, and France produce the largest number of professional players in this dataset, reflecting the scale and depth of their domestic football pipelines.



International caps vs. market value


Players with a high number of international caps tend to carry higher market values, though many high-value players have few or no caps at all.



Distribution of player ages


Most ages from about 24 to 34 have roughly 1,500 to 1,700 players each, then the count drops sharply after 35. Very few players are under 18 or over 40.

title: PCA
text:
PCA is a way to simplify data that has a lot of columns. Many columns end up telling the same story. For example, players who score more also tend to assist more, and players with more international caps tend to be worth more. PCA combines the original columns into a smaller set of new ones, called principal components. The first component points in the direction where players differ the most. The second points in the next biggest direction that is at a right angle to the first, and so on. The components don’t overlap with each other.
Under the hood, the directions are the eigenvectors of the data’s covariance matrix, and the eigenvalues say how much of the variation each direction holds. A big eigenvalue means that component matters a lot. The numbers inside an eigenvector, called loadings, show how much each original column contributes. The same result also comes from the singular value decomposition (SVD). PCA is just the SVD of the centered data, with the squared singular values (divided by n − 1) giving the eigenvalues.
Dimensionality reduction means keeping only the first few components, so the data can be described with fewer columns and lose as little as possible. This matters because data with many columns is hard to work with. It can’t be plotted, columns repeat each other, distances stop being meaningful as columns pile up, and models can overfit. Fewer dimensions make the data easier to see, explore and model. Here, PCA shows how many separate ideas are hiding in the eight player features and what they mean.
Goals and assists per 90 minutes (both standardized) for 300 players, with the principal axes drawn from the center. PC1 follows the biggest spread and PC2 is at a right angle to it.
Each point is projected onto PC1 (red), turning two dimensions into one. The closer the points are to that line, the less information is lost.

title: Clustering
text:
Clustering is a way to group things that look alike without telling the computer what the groups are. Every player is a row of numbers, and the method puts players with similar numbers together. Since nobody supplies the answer, it works well for finding patterns that were not obvious before.
There are two main styles. In partitional clustering, like k-means, the number of groups (k) is chosen first. The method places k centers in the data, assigns each player to the closest center, moves each center to the middle of its group, and repeats until nothing changes. In hierarchical clustering, every player starts as their own group, and the two closest groups are merged over and over until only one is left. The merges are drawn as a tree called a dendrogram, and cutting the tree at any height gives a set of clusters.
Both styles need a way to measure how close two players are. K-means here uses regular straight-line (Euclidean) distance. The hierarchical clustering uses cosine distance, which looks at the pattern of a player’s numbers instead of how big they are, and it joins groups using the average distance between their members (average linkage).
The plan is to use clustering to look for types of players without ever giving position as an input. If the groups match attackers, defenders and goalkeepers, position shows up on its own in the numbers. If they don’t, something else, like age or international experience, is doing the sorting. Position is only checked afterward.



Partitional clustering: k-means with three centroids


A small example with three groups. Each point goes to its closest center (the black X), and the centers keep moving until nothing changes.



Hierarchical clustering: example dendrogram


A dendrogram for 25 example points, built by merging the closest groups step by step. The taller a join is, the further apart the groups were.

title: Clustering
text:
Data Prep
Clustering only works on numbers with no labels. Position, name and club were taken out and kept on the side, just to help read the clusters later.
The cleaned data had 27,607 players. Players with fewer than 900 career minutes (about ten full games) were dropped, because rates based on very few minutes are unreliable. That left 17,218 players. Eight features were used: age, height, total minutes, goals per 90 minutes, assists per 90 minutes, yellow cards per 90 minutes, international caps and market value. Minutes, caps and market value are very skewed, so they were put on a log scale. All eight were then standardized (mean of 0, standard deviation of 1) so that big numbers don’t outweigh small ones.
Hierarchical clustering has to compare every pair of players, which is too much for 17,000 rows, so a random sample of 2,000 players was used for all the clustering. Using the same sample for both methods keeps the comparison fair. No player in the sample had all zeros, which cosine distance needs.



Sample of the clustering data in original units


The first rows of the 2,000-player sample in original units. Every column is a number, and there are no labels or missing values.



The same sample after standardization


The same rows after standardizing. This is the version that goes into the clustering.

Code
The code for this tab is in the clustering and PCA notebook. It is written in Python, using pandas and NumPy for the data, scikit-learn for k-means and silhouette scores, SciPy for the hierarchical clustering and dendrogram, and matplotlib and seaborn for the figures.

title: Clustering
text:
Results

K-means
K-means was run for every k from 2 to 8. Three values were looked at closely: k = 2 (the best silhouette score), k = 4 (a soft bend in the elbow plot, and it matches the four broad positions) and k = 6 (a small bump in the silhouette score). The elbow plot goes down smoothly with no clear bend, so it doesn’t pick k on its own.



K-means elbow plot


Inertia (how spread out players are inside their clusters) falls steadily as k grows. There is no sharp bend, so the plot alone doesn’t settle the best k.
The silhouette score checks how well each player fits their own cluster compared to the next closest one. It runs from -1 to 1, and higher is better. The best score is at k = 2 (0.20). It drops to about 0.16 at k = 3 and 4, bumps up a little at k = 6 (0.15), and ends near 0.14 at k = 8. So the best k by silhouette is 2, but all the scores are low, meaning the clusters overlap quite a bit.



K-means silhouette scores


The average silhouette score is highest at k = 2 and then drops, with a small bump at k = 6. All the scores are low, so the clusters are not sharply separated.
To see what is inside each cluster, the features were averaged per cluster and compared with position, which was not used to build them.
At k = 2, position doesn’t matter much, since every position shows up in both groups. The split is between younger players with international experience (average age about 26, around 8 caps, value near 3 million euros) and older players with hardly any caps and lower value (average age about 31, value near 235,000 euros).
At k = 4, the groups line up with roles and career stages:

Goal scorers and creators: the most goals (0.24) and assists (0.17) per 90, mostly attackers and midfielders, average age about 31.
Young prospects: average age 24.5, tall, low output, but already worth more than most (about 1.2 million euros).
Older defensive veterans: average age 33, the lowest goals, assists and value, mostly defenders and goalkeepers.
Elite internationals: the most minutes, about 20 caps and the highest value (about 3.7 million euros), from all positions.

At k = 6 the groups get more specific. One group picks up far more yellow cards than the rest (about double). Another is young with the highest goals, assists and value (about 5.8 million euros). Another has the most minutes and around 24 caps, and another is older and productive but with almost no caps and low value.
To draw the clusters, the eight features were squeezed down to two (using PCA, covered on the next tab), which only shows about 46% of the information. The groups look separate at k = 2 and k = 4 but overlap a lot at k = 6, partly because two dimensions can’t show everything.



K-means clusters at k = 2, 4 and 6


K-means clusters for k = 2, 4 and 6 on the first two principal components (46% of the variation). The groups are clear at k = 2 and 4 and overlap a lot at k = 6.


Hierarchical clustering
Hierarchical clustering used cosine distance and average linkage on the same 2,000 players. The dendrogram has one big split at the top, and each branch splits again, which gives four main groups. The silhouette score (using cosine distance) is highest at k = 2 (0.25), falls to about 0.16 at k = 7, and goes back up a bit to 0.19 at k = 8. So hierarchical clustering also points to k = 2, with k = 4 as the next sensible level.



Hierarchical clustering dendrogram


Dendrogram using cosine distance, cut down to the last 30 merges (the numbers in brackets are players in each branch). It splits in two at the top, and each side splits again into four main groups.


Comparing the two methods
For a fair comparison, k-means was also scored with cosine distance. K-means scores higher at every k (for example 0.27 vs 0.20 at k = 4), and all the curves agree that k = 2 is the cleanest split. The adjusted Rand index (ARI) measures how much two clusterings agree, where 1 means identical and 0 means no better than chance. It is 0.59 at k = 2, 0.48 at k = 4 and 0.35 at k = 6. So the methods agree on the big picture and drift apart as k grows.
At k = 4, about 90% of the older defensive veterans end up in one hierarchical group, about 95% of the elite internationals in another, and about 75% of the goal scorers and creators in a third. The young prospects are the least stable and get split mostly across two groups. The hierarchical method also finds a small group of 138 players that k-means doesn’t have a match for.



Silhouette comparison: k-means and hierarchical clustering


Silhouette scores for k-means (Euclidean and cosine) and hierarchical clustering (cosine). All peak at k = 2, and on the same cosine measure k-means beats hierarchical at every k.

title: Clustering
text:
Conclusions
Soccer players don’t split into neat, separate types. The silhouette scores are low everywhere (under 0.3, and about 0.20 at best for k-means with regular distance), and the clusters blur into each other, so players look more like a smooth spread than separate boxes.
Even so, a few types keep showing up in both methods: older defensive veterans with low output and low value, young prospects, productive attackers and creators, and an elite group of experienced internationals. Age and international experience separate these groups more than position does. Position was never used, and the cleanest split (k = 2) cuts across every position.
For the question of what drives a player’s value, the clusters suggest that age, international experience and output all move along with market value. That gives the later models some good things to test.

title: PCA
text:
PCA is a way to simplify data that has a lot of columns. Many columns end up telling the same story. For example, players who score more also tend to assist more, and players with more international caps tend to be worth more. PCA combines the original columns into a smaller set of new ones, called principal components. The first component points in the direction where players differ the most. The second points in the next biggest direction that is at a right angle to the first, and so on. The components don’t overlap with each other.
Under the hood, the directions are the eigenvectors of the data’s covariance matrix, and the eigenvalues say how much of the variation each direction holds. A big eigenvalue means that component matters a lot. The numbers inside an eigenvector, called loadings, show how much each original column contributes. The same result also comes from the singular value decomposition (SVD). PCA is just the SVD of the centered data, with the squared singular values (divided by n − 1) giving the eigenvalues.
Dimensionality reduction means keeping only the first few components, so the data can be described with fewer columns and lose as little as possible. This matters because data with many columns is hard to work with. It can’t be plotted, columns repeat each other, distances stop being meaningful as columns pile up, and models can overfit. Fewer dimensions make the data easier to see, explore and model. Here, PCA shows how many separate ideas are hiding in the eight player features and what they mean.



PCA: principal axes of correlated data


Two related variables with their principal axes. PC1 points along the biggest spread, and PC2 is at a right angle to it.



Dimensionality reduction: projecting 2D data onto one component


Each point is projected onto PC1 (red), which turns two dimensions into one. Since the points lie close to that line, not much is lost.

Data Prep

Position, name and club are not part of the PCA and are only used later to color the plots.

text:
Code
The code for this tab is in the clustering and PCA notebook. It is written in Python, using pandas and NumPy for the data, scikit-learn for PCA, NumPy for the SVD check, and matplotlib and seaborn for the figures.

title: PCA
text:
Results

How much variation each component holds
The first component explains 26.6% of the variation, the second 19.7%, the third 16.8% and the fourth 12.5%. Added up, that is 63.1% by PC3, 75.6% by PC4, 85.5% by PC5 and 92.1% by PC6. No single component takes over, so the differences between players are spread across several separate ideas.
Three components have an eigenvalue above 1 (2.13, 1.58 and 1.34), which is a common rule of thumb for how many to keep, and a fourth is right at 1 (0.996). Four components keep about three quarters of the information, and it takes six to pass 90%. Running PCA on all 17,218 players gives almost the same percentages (26.8, 18.8, 16.9 and 12.6), so the 2,000-player sample is a fair stand-in.



PCA scree plot


Bars show the variation explained by each component, and the line shows the running total. No component dominates, four reach about 76%, and it takes six to pass 90%.


What the components mean
The loadings show how much each feature contributes to each component:

PC1, overall prominence: market value (0.57), caps (0.47), assists (0.38) and goals (0.33) go up together, and age goes the other way (-0.38). A high score means a younger, productive, valuable player with international experience.
PC2, attacking output vs. height: assists (0.50), age (0.49) and goals (0.37) go up together, while height (-0.44) and market value (-0.29) go the other way. High scores are older attacking players, and low scores are taller players with less output.
PC3, playing time: minutes (0.68), age (0.43), height (0.32) and caps (0.31) go up together, and yellow cards go down (-0.30).
PC4, discipline: yellow cards per 90 is 0.80 and everything else is small. This matches the card-heavy group found in the k = 6 clustering.

The sign of a component doesn’t mean anything on its own, because flipping every sign gives the same result. What matters is which variables move together and which move against each other.



PCA loadings heatmap


How much each feature contributes to the first four components. PC1 is mostly value, caps and output, and PC4 is almost entirely yellow cards.


Players and features together
In the biplot, each arrow shows which way a feature pulls. Arrows pointing the same way are related (goals, assists and minutes; market value and caps), and arrows pointing opposite ways move against each other (age vs. value and caps; height vs. goals and assists). Players are colored by position, which PCA never saw. Goalkeepers and defenders sit toward the lower left, away from value and output. Attackers spread to the right and upper right along the goals, assists and value arrows, and midfielders overlap both groups. There is still a lot of overlap, which makes sense because two components cover only 46% of the variation.



PCA biplot colored by position


Players on PC1 and PC2, colored by position, with arrows for each feature. Goalkeepers and defenders sit on the left and attackers spread to the right, even though position was never given to PCA.
As a check, the SVD of the centered data was calculated directly. The squared singular values divided by n − 1 match the PCA eigenvalues exactly, and the singular vectors match the loadings (up to sign). So PCA and SVD give the same answer.

title: PCA
text:
Conclusions
The numbers suggest that player profiles come from several separate things instead of one: how prominent a player is (value and caps), attacking output versus size, playing time and experience, and discipline. No single one explains more than about a quarter of the differences, which fits the clustering result that players are spread out smoothly instead of falling into clear groups.
Four components keep about three quarters of the information, so the eight features can be cut down to four without losing too much, which will help with later models. PCA never saw position, but goalkeepers, defenders and attackers still spread out on the first two components, so role differences show up in the numbers by themselves. Market value is also most strongly tied to the first component, next to caps and output, so value seems linked more to prominence and international exposure than to any one stat.
